text: Two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, many minors, were detained during protests in Milan over rising living costs, officials said. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence while Mayor Giuseppe Sala said the damage was unjustifiable.

sources.title: Weekend of fiery protests in France raises questions, costs millions - DW.com
sources.articleText:
In Limoges, France, rioters set the historic town hall on fire, while in Lyon it was the city's tourism information center. In Paris, protesters tried to break into the Elysee Palace; in Marseille and Avignon, they attacked a police station and the prefecture building, respectively.
French President Emmanuel Macron sharply criticized protesters who had turned to violence. "Those who looted will have to pay for the damage and those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable," Macron said in a televised address on Sunday night. Roughly 2,400 people were arrested in France over the weekend.
Estimates for the total number of protesters across France ranged from 550,000 to 800,000. In Paris, people initially gathered peacefully at the Place de la Republique on Saturday. The protest centered on the high price of gas and a call for better conditions in French schools.
Soon, however, it became clear that some of the people in the streets wanted to express their anger in violent ways. Some threw stones, looted stores and set buildings on fire.
A shop owner in Paris told the BBC they did not think the people looting shops were genuine protesters, but individuals taking advantage of the unrest. Security camera footage showed young people breaking into mobile phone shops and helping themselves.
Sports stores like Decathlon and Intersport were also looted. An Apple store, branches of famed department store Galeries Lafayette and luxury labels Celine, Rolex, Louis Vuitton and Christian Dior were also targeted. Galeries Lafayette told industry publication Women's Wear Daily that it had closed early as a precaution and that its Bordeaux branch was worst impacted.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu blamed the "ultra-left" and criminals for the violence. According to the French Interior Ministry, roughly 500 police, firefighters and paramedics were injured over the weekend. In the southern French city of Saint-Etienne, a 17-year-old boy lost his right hand to a crowd control grenade.
Because of the high deficit and the state's high debt, the French government doesn't have a lot of room to react to the protesters' demands. The National Assembly is currently debating the 2027 budget, which includes cuts that are projected at around €45 billion ($50.5 billion).
In the aftermath of the violence, it was estimated that around 1,500 businesses in France had been damaged and that business owners were looking at losses in the hundreds of millions of euros.
On Monday, Parisians awoke to scenes of destruction after groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire. "It's like we had a war," one Paris resident told news agency AFP. It was "terrifying," another added.
In central Milan, Italy, what started as a peaceful march to protest rising living costs on Saturday ended with masked people throwing stones and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables.
There was further damage and violence on Sunday, with black-clad youths seen ransacking a supermarket and other shops. Bus shelters and parked cars were also damaged. Local news agencies reported that at least two police officers were injured and about 50 demonstrators, including many minors, were detained.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said holding demonstrations was a democratic right but that "setting our cities on fire is not." On social media, she blamed "hooligans" for exploiting the protests. Milan Mayor Giuseppe Sala argued that while he understood the reasons for the protests, "violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable."
In the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, a protest that drew tens of thousands of demonstrators upset about rising costs and the housing crisis ended with an informal, overnight camp being built in a central square. A similar camp in northern city of Porto had already been removed by authorities.
Portuguese demonstrators say low wages are failing to keep pace with the rising cost of living. Portugal's inflation was at 3.6% in September and Portuguese housing prices went up by 124% between 2015 and 2024, about twice as much as the EU average. Rents for new leases have nearly doubled since 2017, news agency Reuters reported.
Similar protests in Spain in late September also saw a tent city established in Madrid's central Puerta del Sol plaza. More than 1,000 tents are thought to have been erected there following protests after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen from her home in Madrid. The encampment remains even as municipal authorities call for its removal.
